catalog_quote: 5.4.2 Stress. Stress occurs on the last syllable of a word if the same pitch is on all syllables. In a word with various pitches, stress occurs on the highest pitch. In a word with two pitches of the same height which are the highest in the word, stress occurs on the syllable closest to the end of the word. [p. 86] ... 5. SUPRASEGMENTALS. There are two level pitches in Obokuitai, represented by /1/ (high) and /2/ (low). The downglide /12/ symbolizes a falling pitch. [p. 81] ... In the following examples, pitches [1'] and [12'] represent slightly higher pitches than [1] and [12]. Syllables with the single vowel /i/ possess this higher pitch. [p. 82] ... 4.1 The Syllable. tone_statements.quote: Other languages with culminative, but non-obligatory /H/ include Somali (and several related Cushitic languages), Agiribi Kiwai (Wurm, 1973; Donohue, 1997), Yucatec Mayan (Gussenhoven, 2007), and Ocaina [Witotoan; Peru] (Agnew and Pike, 1957). While /HL/ but not /H/ is culminative in Obokuitai [Lakes Plain; Indonesia (Papua)] (Jenison and Jen- ison, 1991), both /H/ and /HL/ (and /LH/ if the word is monosyllabic) are culminative in Puinave [isolate; Colombia] (Guirón Higuita and Wetzels, 2007), as seen in (14).
tone_statements.summary: Cites Obokuitai (after Jenison & Jenison 1991) as a tone system in which the falling /HL/ tone, but not /H/, is culminative (at most one per word); gives no inventory, forms or analysis.

sources.citation: Clouse, Duane A. 1997. Towards a reconstruction and reclassification of the Lakes Plain languages of Irian Jaya. In Karl Franklin (ed.), Papers in Papuan linguistics No. 2, 133-236. Pacific Linguistics A-85. Canberra: ANU.
sources.quote: p. 152: 'Tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages ... All the modern languages have at least high and low tone. ... Obokuitai has a fall (Jenison 1991)'. p. 160: 'stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date.'
sources.locator: sec. 11 'Tone typology', p. 152; Appendix 3 intro, p. 160
sources.note: Only other published work touching Obokuitai prosody; confirms the tone inventory (H, L, fall) after Jenison 1991 and states stress is non-contrastive across Lakes Plain, supporting a caution that Obokuitai 'stress' is derivative of lexical pitch.

sources.note: Uses Obokuitai as one of three illustrative languages in the opening example (1) of traditional tone transcription: monosyllables contrasting H (kuik1 'rock'), L (kuik2 'insect (sp.)') and HL falling (kuik12 'lizard (sp.)'), with numerals 1 = high, 2 = low, 12 = fall, data credited to Jenison & Jenison 1991:85; no LH rising form is given for Obokuitai (the Awa and Falam columns have one). No further discussion of Obokuitai in the paper; secondary citation only.
